text: Have I published any critical scholarship on Mormonism? Hey everybody, I'm Dan Mlelen. I'm a scholar of the Bible and religion, and we will return
to our regularly scheduled programming soon enough, but I've gotten this question an awful lot over the last 24 hours, and I thought I would address it
because I have published some critical scholarship on Mormonism. Most of these have been in LDS venues, journals, and
at LDS conferences, and things like that. But the scholarship is critical.
And I'll start with this paper from the journal interpreter. I think this was published in 2015. Psalm 82 in contemporary Latter-day Saint tradition.
But in this paper, I talk about what's going on in Psalm 82, what's going on in John 10's quotation of Psalm 82 and how
Latter-day Saints have negotiated with those different understandings to create their own understanding of what's going
on in Psalm 82. There's also this 2019 paper from a journal called Religious Educator. as far as it is translated
correctly, Bible translation and the church. And this is a review article based on Tom Weman's new translation of
the New Testament that was published several years ago. But I use the opportunity to also talk about Bible translation, what Latter-day Saints
generally don't know about Bible translation and how this new translation fits into Latter-day Saint engagement
with the Bible in English. And then in 2020, I published this paper in the Journal of Book of Mormon Studies.
Second Nephi 25:23 in literary and rhetorical context. And this is a very famous or infamous passage in the Book of Mormon that concludes, "For we know
that it is by grace that we are saved after all we can do." And this has historically been read as an indication that grace is not operative until after
we've exhausted all of our efforts and done all that we can do. And in the paper I go through the use of that
phrase after all we can do in the late 18th and early 19th centuries and demonstrate
that anyone who read this in that time period would have understood this phrase to mean precisely despite all we can do.
In other words, this passage is not about a worksbased sotariology. It is
precisely about grace saving us irrespective of anything we could ever do. Another contribution of mine is
actually just a YouTube video of mine. I haven't revised the paper and submitted it for publication anywhere but I might.
You can find it if you look for perfect revelation and the capacity of the people. It's from about 3 years ago and it's basically talking about doctrine in
covenants 138 which says what I the Lord have spoken I have spoken and I excuse not myself. And though the heavens and
the earth pass away, my word shall not pass away, but shall all be fulfilled, whether by my known voice or by the
voice of my servants, it is the same, which has been historically interpreted as an indication that the voice of the prophets is isometric with God's voice.
In other words, if a prophet says it, you should understand that as God saying that. And what I demonstrate in that discussion is that that's not actually
what it's saying. It's saying whether it is fulfilled by my voice or the voice of my prophets, the prophecy, whatever
promise was made is fulfilled all the same. The fulfillment stands whether the fulfillment takes place at God's own hands or at the hands of God's prophets.
And then something that is being published by a secular press is this book called Mormonism in 5 minutes that
I have edited. It will come out in September of this year, published by Equinox Press, which is a UK-based
academic press. And this gathers uh I forget exactly how many, 75 to 80 essays that are each intended to be read within
about 5 minutes. And they're supposed to be very accessible essays. And the description here says, Mormonism in 5 minutes provides an accessible introduction to the origins, ideologies,
and practices of Mormonism in its different forms. It comprises brief and readable essays that answer common questions that those unfamiliar with the
tradition might ask, including, is Mormonism Christian? What is the relationship of the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints to Mormonism? How did the Mormon scriptural
cannon develop? Why does the Book of Mormon quote so much the Book of Isaiah?
What do members of the Community of Christ believe about the Book of Mormon? Do some Mormons still practice polygamy?

couldn't black people enter Latterday Saint temples until 1978?
And so on. So if you would like a publication from me that directly and critically addresses a bunch of
different questions related to Mormonism that is published by a secular press, uh that book I think will be very useful to
a general public and again comes out in September. I will keep everybody posted on the progress of that book because I
